about: The dismissal. Missa is a late Latin form of the noun missio — a dismissal, as collecta stands beside collectio — and from this one word the whole liturgy took its name. The sentence is ordinary and complete: Ite — go, Missa est — the dismissal is made. The rubric directs that the dismissal be chosen “pro Missæ qualitate”, according to the character of the Mass: beside Ite, Missa est it names Benedicámus Dómino (“Let us bless the Lord”), and in Masses for the Dead it directs Requiéscant in pace (“May they rest in peace”) with the answer Amen. At a sung Mass the dismissal is sung: the books give it several melodies, and in the Easter octave a form of its own with a double allelúia.

s01.narrative: After the last prayer following Communion the priest says:

s04.narrative: And according to the character of the Mass the priest says either Ite, Missa est or Benedicámus Dómino (“Let us bless the Lord”); to both the answer is Deo grátias.

s05.translation: Go forth, the Mass is ended.

s07.narrative: In Masses for the Dead the priest says instead: may they rest in peace — and the answer is Amen.

w002.function: One written word carrying two: the preposition cum stands after the pronoun and fuses with it, as it always does with the personal pronouns (mecum, tecum, nobíscum).

w007.function: Plural: the command is addressed to the assembly, not to one person.

w008.function: Nominative, not ablative — it is the subject, and “est” (w009) the verb. The same form could be an ablative, but then the sentence would have no subject at all.

w010.function: Dative, not ablative: thanks are rendered TO someone. The two cases are spelled alike here.

w011.function: Accusative plural governed by a verb never spoken: in full the phrase would be grátias agámus, “let us give thanks”, as in the dialogue before the Preface.
